UNIT 4 / WEEK 1 / CHAPTER 1

Refining relational database designs

Turn requirements and dependencies into a six-table model, then check what the keys and constraints actually enforce.

DATABASE DESIGN CLASSROOM DRAFT · REVIEW PENDING

What you’ll learn

  • Identify anomalies and functional dependencies in a flat relation.
  • Read/create crow’s-foot relationships and resolve many-to-many with a composite bridge.
  • Represent optional one-to-one attendance and its paired foreign key.
  • Reconcile a data dictionary with SQLite enforcement and remaining business rules.

1. Refine from requirements, not a table count

Start by writing what the community centre needs to record. A workshop describes an activity. A session is one scheduled delivery of that workshop.

  • Each session has exactly one workshop and one instructor.
  • A member can book several sessions. A session can have several members.
  • A member can book a particular session only once.
  • A booking can have one attendance record later. No attendance record means “not recorded yet”, rather than “absent”.

You can store an instructor or workshop before creating sessions. You can also store a member or session before creating bookings. Names and titles need not be unique.

Give each session a positive capacity. Checking that all bookings fit within it is a separate business rule: a requirement that involves counting several rows. The six tables here serve different purposes. The Year 12 implementation requires at least five tables, but a table count alone does not make a design sound. This clinic prepares you for the later database project.

2. Diagnose a flat record and its dependencies

Imagine storing every booking in one large table. A row contains MemberID, MemberName, SessionID, SessionDate, Capacity, WorkshopID, WorkshopTitle, InstructorID, InstructorName, BookedOn and Present. You identify a booking with the pair (MemberID, SessionID).

Ask which identifier determines each value. MemberID determines MemberName. SessionID determines the session details. A rule such as “MemberID determines MemberName” is a functional dependency.

  • Partial dependency: MemberName needs only MemberID, which is part of the booking key. Session details need only SessionID. These dependencies prevent second normal form (2NF).
  • Transitive dependency: SessionID leads to WorkshopID, which leads to WorkshopTitle. InstructorName has a similar indirect dependency through InstructorID.

Repeated details cause anomalies, or problems when you change data. Updating an instructor name in many booking rows can leave conflicting names. You cannot insert an unbooked session if bookings are your only storage. Deleting its last booking can also lose the session details.

Normalisation separates facts according to these dependencies. In first normal form (1NF), use one atomic value per field for the defined domain and remove repeating lists. In 2NF, remove non-key partial dependencies on candidate keys. In third normal form (3NF), address the remaining problematic non-key dependencies. State your candidate keys and dependencies before decomposing the table. Adding a surrogate BookingID does not remove those dependencies or the rule against duplicate member/session pairs.

3. Read the six-table crow’s-foot model

RelationshipBoth directions
Workshop–SessionWorkshop has zero or many sessions; each session has exactly one workshop
Instructor–SessionInstructor has zero or many sessions; each session has exactly one instructor
Member–BookingMember has zero or many bookings; each booking has exactly one member
Session–BookingSession has zero or many bookings; each booking has exactly one session
Booking–AttendanceBooking has zero or one attendance record; attendance has exactly one booking

The bridge Booking resolves Member–Session many-to-many. Its composite key stops duplicate bookings for the same pair. Attendance reuses that pair as its primary key and composite foreign key. This permits at most one attendance row per booking, but does not require one to exist.

Optional one-to-one storage is justified here because attendance is recorded later as a separate event. An alternative could store a nullable attendance state on Booking; compare simplicity, meaning and requirements. Do not split a table merely to manufacture a one-to-one relationship.

4. Write relational notation and key rules

Instructor(InstructorID PK, DisplayName)
Workshop(WorkshopID PK, Title)
Session(SessionID PK, WorkshopID FK, InstructorID FK, SessionDate, Capacity)
Member(MemberID PK, DisplayName)
Booking(MemberID PK/FK, SessionID PK/FK, BookedOn)
Attendance(MemberID PK/FK, SessionID PK/FK, Present)
Attendance(MemberID,SessionID) jointly references Booking(MemberID,SessionID).

Read Booking's key as a pair: MemberID and SessionID together identify one booking. A member can book several sessions, and a session can have several members, so neither field identifies a booking on its own. This is a composite key.

Now follow Attendance's foreign key. It refers to the whole Booking pair. Separate references to Member and Session would prove only that each parent exists; they would not prove that this member booked this session.

Mark every field that forms a composite key in the notation. SessionID is a surrogate identifier, so you can record repeated workshop deliveries, even on the same date. The design does not assume that (WorkshopID, SessionDate) is unique. Add that restriction only if the organiser requires it, then document and enforce it. A sample with no duplicates is not evidence that duplicates must be forbidden.

Visual walkthrough

The whole booking pair matters

Suppose M01 and S02 each exist, but the only booking is (M01, S01). Compare what the two reference designs would check.

Pause and predict: If you add Booking(M01, S02), does the joint foreign key require you to create Attendance(M01, S02) immediately?

Show the explanation

No. The booking may have no attendance row. The foreign key checks any attendance row you choose to create; it does not require a child row for every booking.

Try a small change: Change the pair to (M02, S01). Explain separately which parent IDs must exist and which exact Booking row must exist before its attendance can be recorded.

5. Make a data dictionary that matches implementation

Use a data dictionary to explain each field. For every field, record its meaning, type, storage format, allowed values, whether it can be NULL, key role and where its rules are enforced. The supplied dictionary covers all 17 columns.

Choose a type from the requirement. Names are text; capacity is an integer; Present is a Boolean state. A duration may need a float. A fixed currency amount can use integer minor units to avoid binary rounding. A date is conceptually a date even when you store it as text.

In this SQLite schema, dates use TEXT and Present uses INTEGER 0 or 1. Ordinary SQLite column declarations provide type affinity: a preferred storage type, rather than a universal rigid type rule. The typeof and range checks add explicit restrictions for capacity and Present. VARCHAR(60) alone does not limit text length in SQLite.

Read each constraint carefully. The name/title CHECK expressions limit trimmed length, but do not trim the stored values. Date fields are NOT NULL, but the schema does not check calendar validity. A malformed date can still be stored. ID formats, session clashes, capacity across bookings and date order also need further constraints or application/transaction logic. Record these gaps rather than calling an unenforced design rule “database validation”.

6. Distinguish three kinds of integrity

Try to insert a duplicate booking, an unknown member reference and a negative capacity. Each challenges a different kind of integrity, meaning a rule that keeps the data structurally sound.

  • Entity integrity: a row's primary key must be unique and non-null.
  • Referential integrity: a required foreign-key reference must point to an existing parent.
  • Domain integrity: a value must belong to its allowed set or range. Capacity must be a positive integer; Present must be in {0, 1}.

A value can pass these checks and still be factually wrong. Present = 1 is allowed, but it does not prove that the member attended.

Enable SQLite foreign-key checking before using the data and verify it for each connection. Changing that setting inside an active transaction has no effect. The schema explicitly adds NOT NULL to required references and TEXT/composite primary-key fields, rather than relying on SQLite's ordinary primary-key behaviour.

In this demonstration, deleting a Booking also deletes its Attendance record: this is a cascading delete. The default reference action blocks deletion of a Member or Session with bookings. These are classroom lifecycle choices. Real records need an agreed retention and authorisation policy before you choose deletion rules.

7. Compare conceptual rules with a runnable schema

Run the offline checker beside the SQL file. It creates an in-memory database, displays table counts and checks whether a proposed attendance pair already has a booking. It does not create a school database or change existing files.

python unit4-design-check.py

-- Example constraint, with both key columns:
FOREIGN KEY(MemberID, SessionID)
    REFERENCES Booking(MemberID, SessionID)

Inspect the schema before executing it in a DBMS. Use an empty disposable database if running the SQL directly; table names can conflict with an existing database. Predict which failures the schema catches, and which it leaves open. Cross-row capacity enforcement and ACID transaction reasoning will be developed later.

8. Transfer to a fresh design

Design a fictional exhibition system: an Artist has zero or many Exhibits; each Exhibit has one Artist. A Visitor can reserve many Exhibits and an Exhibit can be reserved by many Visitors; each pair occurs once. Each Reservation may receive one CheckIn record. Add a Venue entity: each Exhibit belongs to one Venue, which may host many Exhibits. Create six tables, notation, a dictionary and crow’s-foot diagram.

Explain the composite reference for CheckIn and a rule that remains unenforced. Compare the model with the workshop system, using fresh identifiers and meanings rather than renaming the diagram mechanically. Record an insertion/update/deletion anomaly in a flat alternative, then show which dependency your decomposition removes.

9. Interpreting a ten-table ER model

Use this ten-table model to practice reading relationships. Follow one connection at a time, explain what it allows, then try the questions before opening the answers. This is optional practice with no marks, submissions or progress records.

Read the model in words

  • Venue has zero or many Room rows; every Room row belongs to exactly one Venue.
  • Room has zero or many Session rows; every Session row belongs to exactly one Room.
  • Workshop has zero or many Session rows; every Session row belongs to exactly one Workshop.
  • Instructor has zero or many Session rows; every Session row belongs to exactly one Instructor.
  • Session has zero or many Booking rows; every Booking row belongs to exactly one Session.
  • Member has zero or many Booking rows; every Booking row belongs to exactly one Member.
  • Session has zero or many SessionEquipment rows; every SessionEquipment row belongs to exactly one Session.
  • Equipment has zero or many SessionEquipment rows; every SessionEquipment row belongs to exactly one Equipment.
  • A booking has zero or one Attendance row; every Attendance row belongs to exactly one Booking.

Each parent table uses unique IDs. A name, room label or date is not assumed to be unique. Every foreign key shown must contain a value.

Check the other field rules too: Capacity and QuantityUsed are positive integers; StockQuantity is zero or a positive integer; Present is 0 or 1.

In each bridge table, the two PK/FK fields work together as one composite primary key. Attendance must refer to an existing Booking pair. Its joint foreign key checks the Member and Session together, not separately.

Worked example: from a booking to a venue

To locate the venue of a booked session, follow Member → Booking → Session → Room → Venue. For example, Booking(M07, S12) refers to Session S12. If S12 has RoomID R02 and R02 has VenueID V01, the booked session is at V01. Each booking identifies one session and that session identifies one room and venue. This does not mean a member can attend only one venue: different bookings can follow different paths.

Relational notation

Venue(VenueID PK, VenueName)
Room(RoomID PK, VenueID FK, RoomLabel, Capacity)
Workshop(WorkshopID PK, Title)
Instructor(InstructorID PK, DisplayName)
Session(SessionID PK, WorkshopID FK, InstructorID FK, RoomID FK, SessionDate, Capacity)
Member(MemberID PK, DisplayName)
Booking(MemberID PK/FK, SessionID PK/FK, BookedOn)
Attendance(MemberID PK/FK, SessionID PK/FK, Present)
Equipment(EquipmentID PK, ItemName, StockQuantity)
SessionEquipment(SessionID PK/FK, EquipmentID PK/FK, QuantityUsed)
Attendance(MemberID, SessionID) jointly references Booking(MemberID, SessionID).

Stored-key snapshot for question 9

Member IDs: M07, M08
Session IDs: S12, S13
Equipment IDs: E01, E02
Booking pairs: (M07,S12), (M07,S13), (M08,S12)
Attendance pairs: (M07,S12), with Present = 1
SessionEquipment pairs: (S12,E01), (S13,E01), each with QuantityUsed = 2

1. Read the whole model

Name the ten tables. Which two are bridge tables, and which table stores an optional follow-up event?

Show explained answer

The tables are Venue, Room, Workshop, Instructor, Session, Member, Booking, Attendance, Equipment and SessionEquipment. Booking bridges Member–Session; SessionEquipment bridges Session–Equipment. Attendance stores an optional follow-up event for a booking.

2. Read a relationship both ways

Read Venue–Room in both directions. Can a venue exist before any rooms are recorded? Can a room exist without a venue?

Show explained answer

A venue has zero or many rooms; each room has exactly one venue. An empty venue is allowed. A room needs a non-null VenueID referring to an existing Venue. The diagram does not require every venue to have a room.

3. Separate a workshop from a session

Why are Workshop and Session separate? Could one workshop run twice, in different rooms, with different instructors?

Show explained answer

Workshop describes the activity; Session describes one scheduled delivery. Two Session rows can reference the same WorkshopID while using different SessionIDs, RoomIDs, InstructorIDs and dates. The model does not impose unique titles or unique workshop/date combinations.

4. Follow several links

Session S12 refers to Room R02; R02 refers to Venue V01. Member M07 is booked in S12 and S13. Does this prove both sessions use V01?

Show explained answer

No. It establishes V01 only for S12. Follow S13’s own RoomID and then that room’s VenueID. The member’s identity does not determine the room or venue of every booking.

5. Resolve two many-to-many relationships

Explain Member–Session and Session–Equipment. Where is each relationship resolved?

Show explained answer

A member can book many sessions and a session can have many members: Booking stores each member/session pair. A session can use several equipment types and an equipment type can be used in several sessions: SessionEquipment stores each session/equipment pair. Both bridges have composite keys that prevent duplicate pairs.

6. Interpret the composite key

Why does SessionEquipment use the pair (SessionID, EquipmentID)? Where should QuantityUsed be stored?

Show explained answer

The pair identifies one equipment type allocated to one session. SessionID alone would permit only one equipment type per session; EquipmentID alone would permit use in only one session. QuantityUsed describes this particular allocation, so it belongs in SessionEquipment, not as a session-independent attribute of Equipment.

7. Interpret optional attendance

Can a booking exist without attendance? Can attendance exist without a booking? Does no attendance row mean Present = 0?

Show explained answer

A booking can have zero or one Attendance row. Each Attendance row must refer to an existing Booking pair. Missing attendance means unrecorded; it is not the same as a recorded Present value of 0. The diagram does not force attendance to be entered later.

8. Use the exact foreign-key target

Why is Attendance’s joint reference to Booking stronger than separate references to Member and Session?

Show explained answer

Separate references establish only that the person and session exist. The composite reference also establishes that this particular person booked this particular session. For example, M08 and S13 may exist while Booking(M08, S13) does not.

9. Check candidate rows

Use the stored-key snapshot below. For each candidate, say whether it is allowed by the stated key/domain rules: Attendance(M07,S13,1); Attendance(M08,S13,1); another Attendance(M07,S12,0); SessionEquipment(S12,E02,1); SessionEquipment(S12,E99,1); SessionEquipment(S13,E02,0).

Show explained answer

Allowed: Attendance(M07,S13,1), because that booking exists and has no attendance; SessionEquipment(S12,E02,1), because both parents exist, the pair is new and quantity is positive. Rejected: Attendance(M08,S13,1), because its booking pair is absent; another Attendance(M07,S12,0), because its primary key already exists; SessionEquipment(S12,E99,1), because E99 is absent; SessionEquipment(S13,E02,0), because zero violates the stated positive-quantity rule. These outcomes assume the stated constraints are enforced.

10. Identify what keys do not enforce

Name three scheduling, capacity or stock rules that these relationships alone do not enforce.

Show explained answer

Possible rules include: a session’s Capacity must not exceed its room’s Capacity; booking count must not exceed session capacity; a room or instructor must not have overlapping sessions; equipment allocations across overlapping sessions must not exceed stock. PK/FK rules do not perform these cross-row checks. Dates alone cannot determine overlap because start time and duration are missing.

11. Trace a report

A report lists member name, workshop title, room label and venue name for each booking. Which six tables must it follow?

Show explained answer

Member → Booking → Session → Workshop gives the member and activity; Session → Room → Venue supplies the location. The six tables are Member, Booking, Session, Workshop, Room and Venue. Attendance and equipment are unnecessary for this report. This is a path-reading exercise, not a requirement to write a six-table SQL join.

12. Check a claim about deletion

A reader says deleting a session must delete all its bookings. Is that specified by the ER diagram?

Show explained answer

No. The relationships say what references must remain valid; they do not choose a deletion policy. A database might restrict deletion, cascade under an explicit rule, or use an agreed archive policy. Do not infer ON DELETE CASCADE from a crow’s foot.

13. Read a one-to-one extension

Explain why Attendance’s primary key limits a booking to one Attendance row. What would need to change to record multiple check-in events?

Show explained answer

Attendance uses the same member/session pair as its primary key, so a second row for that booking duplicates the key. For multiple events, introduce an event identifier or a justified key including an event sequence/time, and change the relationship to Booking 1 → 0..many events. This is a discussion of an extension, not a diagram-creation requirement.

14. Explain a repeated room label

Two rows use RoomLabel “Studio”, one at each of two venues. Is that forbidden by the model?

Show explained answer

No. RoomID identifies the room; RoomLabel is not stated to be unique. If the business requires room labels to be unique within each venue, document a unique constraint on (VenueID, RoomLabel). Do not infer it from sample names.

10. Resolve update, insertion and deletion anomalies with evidence

Begin with business dependencies, not a rule that every repeated value is wrong. In the supplied flat membership table the key is (StudentID, ClubID). StudentID determines StudentName; ClubID determines ClubName and CoachID; CoachID determines CoachPhone. Each student may join many clubs, each club may have many students, and each club currently has one coach.

AnomalyFlat-table problemResolution and check
UpdateChanging T1's phone in only one membership leaves conflicting copiesUpdate one Coach row; all related clubs obtain that phone through a join
InsertionA new club with no members cannot be represented without inventing a student or breaking the membership keyInsert the Club independently, then add Membership rows when students join
DeletionDeleting the last Film membership loses Film's club/coach facts from the flat tableDelete the Membership only; Club and Coach records remain

The rows already have atomic values, so they can be in 1NF while still having anomalies. To reach 2NF for this composite-key design, separate Student and Club facts from Membership because they depend on only part of the key. At that stage Club may still store CoachPhone. To reach 3NF, separate Coach because ClubID determines CoachID which determines CoachPhone. The final relations are Student, Coach, Club and Membership. Keep linking keys and enforce relationships so decomposition does not disconnect facts.

Reconstruct the original memberships with a join before the independent insert/update/delete activities, checking both missing and extra rows. The fixture's repeated facts are consistent; real conflicting records require investigation. SELECT DISTINCT can suppress identical projections but cannot decide which conflicting phone number is true. A repeated foreign key is expected in a one-to-many relationship and is not by itself a normalisation error.

Pause and predict

If the final Film membership is deleted in the flat table, which facts disappear? Should deleting a membership mean the club no longer exists?

SQLITE · WORKED EXAMPLE

Download anomalies_lab.sql

-- Fresh disposable SQLite database. Fixture dependencies are explicitly stated.
PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;
CREATE TABLE FlatMembership (
    StudentID TEXT, StudentName TEXT, ClubID TEXT, ClubName TEXT,
    CoachID TEXT, CoachPhone TEXT,
    PRIMARY KEY (StudentID, ClubID)
);
INSERT INTO FlatMembership VALUES
('S1', 'Ari', 'C1', 'Robotics', 'T1', '200'),
('S2', 'Bo', 'C1', 'Robotics', 'T1', '200'),
('S1', 'Ari', 'C2', 'Film', 'T2', '201');
CREATE TABLE Student (StudentID TEXT PRIMARY KEY, StudentName TEXT NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE Coach (CoachID TEXT PRIMARY KEY, CoachPhone TEXT NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE Club (
    ClubID TEXT PRIMARY KEY, ClubName TEXT NOT NULL,
    CoachID TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES Coach(CoachID)
);
CREATE TABLE Membership (
    StudentID TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES Student(StudentID),
    ClubID TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES Club(ClubID),
    PRIMARY KEY (StudentID, ClubID)
);
-- DISTINCT copies known-consistent fixture facts; it does not resolve conflicts.
INSERT INTO Student SELECT DISTINCT StudentID, StudentName FROM FlatMembership;
INSERT INTO Coach SELECT DISTINCT CoachID, CoachPhone FROM FlatMembership;
INSERT INTO Club SELECT DISTINCT ClubID, ClubName, CoachID FROM FlatMembership;
INSERT INTO Membership SELECT StudentID, ClubID FROM FlatMembership;
-- Capture a reconstruction before the independent modification activities.
CREATE TABLE ReconstructedBefore AS
SELECT s.StudentID, s.StudentName, c.ClubID, c.ClubName, t.CoachID, t.CoachPhone
FROM Membership AS m
JOIN Student AS s ON s.StudentID = m.StudentID
JOIN Club AS c ON c.ClubID = m.ClubID
JOIN Coach AS t ON t.CoachID = c.CoachID;
UPDATE Coach SET CoachPhone = '299' WHERE CoachID = 'T1';
INSERT INTO Club VALUES ('C3', 'Coding', 'T1');
DELETE FROM Membership WHERE StudentID = 'S1' AND ClubID = 'C2';
SELECT ClubID, ClubName FROM Club ORDER BY ClubID;

Build understanding in steps

  1. Guided completion: Draw arrows for each stated dependency. Complete the 1NF → 2NF → 3NF table splits, keeping keys visible. Predict a join that reconstructs each original membership exactly once.
  2. Independent transfer: Use the SQL fixture to add Coding with no members, update T1's phone once, and remove Film's last membership. Verify the club and coach survive. Transfer to Asset(AssetID, AssetName, RoomID, RoomName), where each RoomID determines one RoomName.
  3. Delayed retrieval: Given a new scenario, name the dependency causing each anomaly before proposing a split. Explain why atomic fields alone do not establish 3NF.
Show the explanation and checking guidance

The final Club relation retains C1 Robotics, C2 Film and C3 Coding. C2 has no memberships but still exists. T1's phone becomes 299 in one Coach row. The asset transfer splits Room(RoomID PK, RoomName) and Asset(AssetID PK, AssetName, RoomID FK). Prove the relationships preserve the intended facts; do not delete repeated foreign keys.

The expected-evidence column gives the starting reference. A sound check explains the rule and its limits, not only a pass label. Keep a contrary or invalid case when appropriate, plus an unaffected case after a change. Your own actual-result evidence is still required.

Practice and explain

KEY

Why is (MemberID, SessionID) a useful Booking key?

Show explained answer

It uniquely represents the allowed one-booking-per-member/session rule while each component alone can repeat.

PAIR

Why does Attendance reference Booking jointly?

Show explained answer

Independent Member/Session references would not establish that the particular pair booked; the composite reference does.

OPTIONAL

Does the Attendance foreign key force every booking to have attendance?

Show explained answer

No. Existing attendance must reference a booking, and its key permits at most one; a booking can still have none.

NORMALISE

Does adding BookingID automatically fix partial/transitive dependencies?

Show explained answer

No. The underlying candidate key and dependencies remain; decomposition and constraints must follow the semantics.

VALIDITY

Does NOT NULL date text prove a valid calendar date?

Show explained answer

No. The schema requires a value but does not validate calendar meaning or factual accuracy.

Your practical task

Interpret the worked model both ways, explain its dependencies/keys, predict constraint failures and reconcile the 17-field dictionary. Create the fresh six-table exhibition design with notation, crow’s-foot diagram, constraints and one explicit remaining business-rule gap.

Show illustrative answer / example

Workshop/Instructor each parent Session; Member/Session link through Booking; Attendance has a composite FK to the Booking pair. Optional attendance is zero or one, not mandatory. Separate member/session descriptions from booking dependencies. Duplicate/orphan/domain checks are enforced where declared, but dates/capacity/clashes remain explicit gaps. Transfer the same reasoning to the exhibition requirements.

Check your understanding

What ensures an attendance record belongs to a member/session pair that was actually booked?

Separate references to Member and Session only. A composite foreign key to the Booking pair. A unique workshop title.

Quick-check answer and explanation

A composite foreign key to the Booking pair.

The joint reference checks the specific pair against Booking; two independent parent references cannot establish that booking exists.

Chapter recap

A refined model records meaning: dependencies guide decomposition, keys enforce identity, paired references enforce a relationship, and documentation names the rules still needing implementation. Table count alone does not establish quality.

Suggested classroom sequence
  1. Lesson 1: retrieve relational/normalisation foundations; diagnose the flat booking relation and state dependencies.
  2. Lesson 2: read six-table crow’s-foot model, composite bridge and optional one-to-one; write notation.
  3. Lesson 3: dictionary/integrity/schema reconciliation; predict and check constraints in an offline database.
  4. Lesson 4: independent exhibition-model transfer and explained feedback. Four lessons in semester week 1; no extra project.

1. Define the report’s grain

Before writing SQL, finish this sentence: “One output row represents …”. That unit is the report's grain. A row might represent one booking, one session or one workshop.

Use the unchanged design seed. It has three bookings: M01/S01, M02/S01 and M01/S02. S03 has no booking. M03 exists but has no booking. Attendance records M01/S01 as Present = 1 and M02/S01 as Present = 0. M01/S02 has no attendance record.

For a booking report, expect three rows. For an all-session report, keep S03 even though it has no booking. Write the expected rows first. Then select the tables and joins that match that meaning. The examples use SQLite; check your own DBMS for differences in date handling and concatenation.

2. Join up to four tables and keep keys visible

Read the query as a chain of key matches. Start with one Booking row. Its MemberID finds the member; its SessionID finds the session; the session’s WorkshopID finds the workshop. A qualified name, such as b.SessionID, identifies the table alias and field together.

These are inner joins, so every output row needs all three matches. In this seed, each required reference has exactly one match. The three bookings therefore produce three rows. Start by predicting one row, then check the complete result.

SELECT b.MemberID, m.DisplayName, s.SessionID, w.Title, s.SessionDate
FROM Booking AS b
INNER JOIN Member AS m ON m.MemberID = b.MemberID
INNER JOIN Session AS s ON s.SessionID = b.SessionID
INNER JOIN Workshop AS w ON w.WorkshopID = s.WorkshopID
ORDER BY s.SessionID, b.MemberID;

Booking is the starting grain. Each join follows a declared key: MemberID, SessionID, then WorkshopID. The report has three rows, ordered by session and member. Selecting names alone can hide distinct people with the same label; retain IDs when identity matters.

Aliases shorten qualified names. They do not rename stored columns or change the schema. Specify an ON condition for each relationship; a missing condition can create every combination of rows. DISTINCT can remove legitimate duplicates from the selected view and should not disguise a broken join.

3. Aggregate at the correct grain

SELECT COUNT(*) AS SessionCount, SUM(Capacity) AS TotalPlaces,
       AVG(Capacity) AS MeanPlaces, MIN(Capacity) AS Smallest,
       MAX(Capacity) AS Largest
FROM Session;

Read the first query as a question about sessions, with one input row per session. It returns count 3, total places 7, mean 7/3, minimum 2 and maximum 3. Functions that combine values into a summary are aggregate functions.

  • COUNT(*) counts rows.
  • COUNT(column) counts non-NULL values in that column.
  • SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX ignore NULL inputs.

With no matching input and no GROUP BY, COUNT returns 0; the other ordinary aggregates shown here return NULL. A grouped query with no input may return no groups.

The second query creates one group per SessionID. Its INNER JOIN keeps only sessions with bookings, so the result is S01: 2 and S02: 1. S03 is excluded. Group by identifiers rather than titles that can repeat. Include each selected nonaggregate attribute in GROUP BY, or justify a valid key dependency explicitly. SQLite permits some bare, ungrouped columns, but that shortcut can produce unreliable reports.

SELECT s.SessionID, COUNT(*) AS Bookings
FROM Session AS s
INNER JOIN Booking AS b ON b.SessionID = s.SessionID
GROUP BY s.SessionID
ORDER BY s.SessionID;

4. Preserve zero-booking sessions

Scope: enrichment. LEFT JOIN syntax is additional to the explicitly listed INNER JOIN work. It supports this all-session report. Counting real keys and distinguishing NULL from recorded absence remain important reasoning; do not replace required multiple-table INNER JOIN practice with this extension. Scope and source.

SELECT s.SessionID, COUNT(b.MemberID) AS Bookings
FROM Session AS s
LEFT JOIN Booking AS b ON b.SessionID = s.SessionID
GROUP BY s.SessionID
ORDER BY s.SessionID;

Start from Session because you need every session. Use a LEFT JOIN to keep a session even when it has no matching Booking.

For S03, the join produces one preserved row whose Booking fields are NULL. COUNT(b.MemberID) ignores that NULL and gives 0. COUNT(*) counts the preserved row itself and incorrectly gives 1 booking. The correct report is S01: 2, S02: 1, S03: 0.

Check where you place conditions. A WHERE condition on the joined Booking or Attendance table can remove rows you meant to preserve. To keep every booking but attach only matching presence records, put the presence condition in ON. If you want only bookings recorded as present, WHERE a.Present = 1 is appropriate, as Q9 shows. Let the report requirement decide.

Worked walkthrough

Keep a session even when it has no booking

A LEFT JOIN keeps every row from Session, the table on the left. An unmatched row has NULL in the Booking fields.

Pause and predict: Which count answers “How many bookings does S03 have?”

Show the explanation

COUNT(b.MemberID) gives 0. The preserved session row itself is not a booking.

Try a small change: Imagine adding one valid booking for S03. Predict both counts before running a changed-data test.

5. Calculate and concatenate with aliases

SELECT s.SessionID, s.Capacity, COUNT(b.MemberID) AS Bookings,
       s.Capacity - COUNT(b.MemberID) AS Remaining,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(b.MemberID) / s.Capacity, 1) AS FillPercent
FROM Session AS s
LEFT JOIN Booking AS b ON b.SessionID = s.SessionID
GROUP BY s.SessionID, s.Capacity
ORDER BY s.SessionID;

Calculate a result from the values you have, then give it a clear name. Here Remaining means capacity minus booking count: S01 has 0 places left, S02 has 2 and S03 has 2. AS gives the calculated column an alias, or result label.

FillPercent reports 100.0, 33.3 and 0.0 for those sessions. Multiplying by the real-valued literal 100.0 prevents integer division from truncating the fraction before rounding. This is a report calculation. It does not store a permanent truth or stop another request from booking a place.

The next query joins text using SQLite's || operator. Combining text is concatenation. BookingLabel combines the member's display name with the workshop title. Other SQL dialects can use different syntax.

If a value in a concatenation is NULL, the result is NULL unless you choose a replacement explicitly. Choose display wording that preserves the meaning of missing data rather than inventing a fact.

SELECT b.MemberID, s.SessionID,
       m.DisplayName || ' / ' || w.Title AS BookingLabel
FROM Booking AS b
INNER JOIN Member AS m ON m.MemberID = b.MemberID
INNER JOIN Session AS s ON s.SessionID = b.SessionID
INNER JOIN Workshop AS w ON w.WorkshopID = s.WorkshopID
ORDER BY s.SessionID, b.MemberID;

Visual walkthrough

Calculate places at session grain

Read one row per session. Count an actual booking key, then use that count in the calculations.

Pause and predict: One new booking is added to S02. What should its Remaining and FillPercent become?

Show the explanation

S02 then has two bookings out of three places. Remaining is 3 − 2 = 1. FillPercent is ROUND(100.0 × 2 / 3, 1), giving 66.7.

Try a small change: Describe how the result changes if S03 receives its first booking. Explain why a displayed percentage alone does not enforce capacity when requests arrive together.

6. Respect composite keys and unknown attendance

Scope: required. Correct composite references and interpretation of data are required concepts. The LEFT JOIN implementation used here is a supporting extension; both key columns must still match. Scope and source.

SELECT b.MemberID, b.SessionID, a.Present
FROM Booking AS b
LEFT JOIN Attendance AS a
 ON a.MemberID = b.MemberID AND a.SessionID = b.SessionID
ORDER BY b.SessionID, b.MemberID;

The attendance join needs both MemberID and SessionID. Joining only on MemberID would incorrectly attach M01’s S01 attendance to the S02 booking. Correct Q7 gives 1, 0, NULL for the three booking rows. NULL means no attendance record here; zero means a recorded absence.

SELECT b.SessionID, COUNT(*) AS Bookings,
       COUNT(a.Present) AS Recorded,
       SUM(a.Present) AS PresentCount
FROM Booking AS b
LEFT JOIN Attendance AS a
 ON a.MemberID = b.MemberID AND a.SessionID = b.SessionID
GROUP BY b.SessionID
ORDER BY b.SessionID;

S01 has 2 bookings,2 recorded states and 1 present. S02 has 1 booking,0 recorded states and NULL present sum. COALESCE can replace NULL for display, but cannot turn an unknown state into factual absence. If calculating an attendance rate, state whether the denominator is all bookings or recorded attendance, and guard a zero denominator.

7. Filter rows and groups deliberately

Scope: support booklet. HAVING is shown in the official support booklet (printed p22). It filters completed groups; learn it after core GROUP BY and aggregate practice. It is support-booklet SQL, rather than a separately named unit-content bullet or an optional-only topic. Scope and source.

SELECT s.SessionID, COUNT(b.MemberID) AS Bookings
FROM Session AS s
LEFT JOIN Booking AS b ON b.SessionID = s.SessionID
GROUP BY s.SessionID
HAVING COUNT(b.MemberID) >= 2
ORDER BY s.SessionID;

WHERE filters input rows before aggregation; HAVING filters groups after aggregation. Q8 retains S01 with 2 bookings. A WHERE date filter would first select sessions/bookings in the agreed period, then group those rows. Use unambiguous YYYY-MM-DD text only after dates are validated; text storage alone does not prove calendar validity.

The conceptual reading order is FROM/JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY/aggregates → HAVING → result/order. It helps explain semantics, but is not a promise about the database engine’s execution plan. ORDER BY is required for a reliable displayed order.

8. Diagnose multiplied totals and test changed data

Trace one joined row before summing capacity. When a session has several bookings, its Capacity appears once for each booking. Adding those repeated values overcounts the places.

For W01, the faulty booking-level sum is 2 + 2 + 3 = 7. The correct session-level total is 2 + 3 = 5. SUM(DISTINCT Capacity) happens to give 5 here, but it removes repeated values, not repeated sessions. Two different sessions can legitimately have the same capacity.

  1. State which entity you are counting or summing.
  2. Aggregate at that entity's key before joining another one-to-many set, or keep the report at the correct grain.
  3. Predict results on changed data, then run the query.

Include an unbooked session, unrecorded attendance, equal labels, equal capacities, an empty filtered input and a member with several sessions. A query that runs without an SQL error can still answer the wrong question.

9. Complete the query clinic

Run the offline report runner after predicting outputs. It recreates the database in memory and executes the ten supplied SELECT queries. The expected-results JSON and teacher guide are separate. No existing database files or school records change.

python unit4-sql-runner.py

Download query pack · Workbook · Teacher explanations · Worked SQL. Teacher files are separate, not access-protected.

Sources: SQLite SELECT, SQLite aggregates and 2026 SCSA Year 12 data management. Original classroom draft; independent review and learner evidence remain pending.

10. DDL and DML: change the structure, change the records

DDL changes database structure: CREATE TABLE defines a table, ALTER TABLE changes supported parts of its structure, and DROP TABLE removes a table. DML changes stored records: INSERT adds rows, UPDATE changes matching rows and DELETE removes matching rows. SELECT retrieves data; some classifications call it DQL, while others include retrieval within DML. State the operation's effect rather than relying only on a label.

OperationExample purposeEvidence to inspect
CREATE / ALTERAdd the Item schema and an Active fieldColumn definitions, defaults and rejected invalid data
INSERTAdd two identified itemsKeys, row count and relationship validity
UPDATE ... WHEREChange the cable price onlyTarget record and unchanged camera record
DELETE ... WHERERemove the disposable cable fixtureIts absence and other records' survival
ROLLBACKUndo a trial price changePreviously committed value restored
DROP TABLERemove the Scratch structureTable no longer exists; unlike DELETE, it does not retain an empty table

Run the download only in a fresh disposable SQLite database. Predict the affected rows before modifying data and SELECT the target plus a non-target afterwards. A WHERE clause can still be wrong: its presence alone is not proof of correctness. SQLite uses ALTER TABLE for supported structural changes; do not paste another DBMS's MODIFY syntax without checking its documentation. Transactions manage a related change; authorisation, validation and constraints remain separate responsibilities.

Pause and predict

After the trial camera price update is rolled back, is its price 0 or 40? Does DELETE remove the Item table?

SQLITE · WORKED EXAMPLE

Download ddl_dml_lab.sql

-- Run on a fresh disposable SQLite database, not a school production database.
PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;
CREATE TABLE Supplier (
    SupplierID INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    SupplierName TEXT NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE Item (
    ItemID INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    ItemName TEXT NOT NULL,
    Cost REAL NOT NULL CHECK (Cost >= 0),
    SupplierID INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES Supplier(SupplierID)
);
ALTER TABLE Item ADD COLUMN Active INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1 CHECK (Active IN (0, 1));
INSERT INTO Supplier VALUES (1, 'North Supplies'), (2, 'West Supplies');
INSERT INTO Item (ItemID, ItemName, Cost, SupplierID)
VALUES (1, 'Camera', 40, 1), (2, 'Cable', 10, 1);
UPDATE Item SET Cost = 12 WHERE ItemID = 2;
DELETE FROM Item WHERE ItemID = 2 AND ItemName = 'Cable';
BEGIN TRANSACTION;
UPDATE Item SET Cost = 0 WHERE ItemID = 1;
ROLLBACK;
CREATE TABLE Scratch (Note TEXT);
DROP TABLE Scratch;
SELECT ItemID, ItemName, Cost, Active FROM Item ORDER BY ItemID;

Build understanding in steps

  1. Guided completion: Colour-code schema statements and record statements on paper. For each modification, identify target rows, expected state and one record/structure that should remain unchanged.
  2. Independent transfer: Use a fresh copy. Add an item, update only its cost, reject a negative cost using the constraint, and delete the disposable item. Inspect state after each operation. Compare DELETE FROM Scratch with DROP TABLE Scratch in separate fresh trials.
  3. Delayed retrieval: Without looking at the labels, explain what each SQL statement changes and design an unaffected-row test that would expose a missing or incorrect WHERE.
Show the explanation and checking guidance

The final Item row is (1, Camera, 40, 1). The cable row was removed; rollback restores the camera price. Supplier still contains two rows. Scratch has been dropped. A negative cost is rejected by CHECK and must not alter the previously stored valid row. DELETE changes rows; DROP removes the structure.

Original ungraded teaching addition · 30 October 2026. Technical references: sql · create · update · delete. Download examples and activity pack · Teacher guidance

11. Check your reasoning, test the claim and retain the evidence

Use the cases below as starting points, not a complete test plan. Write the expected outcome before running code, issuing SQL or revealing the explanation. For a conceptual claim, use the scenario and a counterexample; for implemented behaviour, record observed results. If the school has not run a check, label it pending.

Pause and predict

Choose one row and justify the expected outcome without using the program's output as your answer key.

Choose a case and predict first

  • Session with zero bookings
  • One parent with multiple child rows
Show expected evidence and why each case matters
Input / scenarioExpected evidenceWhy this case?
Session with zero bookingsRetained if report requires all sessionsJoin choice
One parent with multiple child rowsAggregate at intended grain without multiplied totalsChanged-data test

Build understanding in steps

  1. Guided completion: Complete the first case with teacher modelling, the second with a partner, then swap explanations and challenge one assumption.
  2. Independent transfer: Create a third case that could expose an error the first two would miss. Record the expected and actual evidence, explain any mismatch, repair one cause and repeat both the new case and earlier cases.
  3. Delayed retrieval: Return after another topic and attempt a changed case without viewing the worked explanation. Explain what transferred and what still needs support.
Show the explanation and checking guidance

The expected-evidence column gives the starting reference. A sound check explains the rule and its limits, not only a pass label. Keep a contrary or invalid case when appropriate, plus an unaffected case after a change. Your own actual-result evidence is still required.

Original ungraded teaching addition · 30 October 2026. Download examples and activity pack · Teacher guidance

Practice and explain

GRAIN

Why does summing capacity after a booking join overcount?

Show explained answer

A session appears once per booking. Sum at session grain, not booking grain. DISTINCT capacity is not a general fix.

ZERO

Why count b.MemberID rather than * after the session LEFT JOIN?

Show explained answer

The unmatched session still has one placeholder row, but its booking key is NULL; COUNT(column) excludes that NULL.

PAIR

Can Attendance join on MemberID alone?

Show explained answer

No. A member can book multiple sessions; both parts of the composite key must match.

NULL

Does NULL attendance mean a recorded absence?

Show explained answer

No. This scenario uses NULL for a missing attendance record and 0 for a recorded absence.

FILTER

Which clause filters groups based on an aggregate count?

Show explained answer

HAVING; WHERE filters input rows before aggregation.

Your practical task

Predict and run the ten reports, implement independent transfer queries, repair missing-key/COUNT*/SUM errors and test changed data. Record report grain, expected rows, actual results and a limited conclusion for each.

Show illustrative answer / example

Use the answer guide: Q1 and Q6 each have three rows; Q3 excludes S03, while Q4 includes it with a count of 0. Q5 gives fill percentages of 100, 33.3 and 0. Composite attendance joins produce 1, 0 and NULL. W01 capacity at session grain is 5, rather than the incorrect booking-join total of 7. Validate changes with independently predicted data.

Check your understanding

How should a report count bookings for an unbooked session preserved by LEFT JOIN?

COUNT(*) so the placeholder row counts as a booking. COUNT(b.MemberID) so NULL booking keys are excluded. SUM(DISTINCT s.Capacity) to count its places.

Quick-check answer and explanation

COUNT(b.MemberID) so NULL booking keys are excluded.

The preserved row has a NULL booking key. COUNT(column) excludes NULL; COUNT(*) counts the row.

Chapter recap

A reliable query follows keys, declares its grain and treats zero, NULL and duplicate-looking labels carefully. Test changed data to expose reports that only happen to work on the sample.

  1. Week 2 lesson 1: retrieve schema/keys and predict four-table joins.
  2. Week 2 lesson 2: implement joins/aliases and diagnose missing conditions.
  3. Week 2 lesson 3: aggregate at session/booking grain; grouped inner reports.
  4. Week 2 lesson 4: zero-booking LEFT JOIN/count clinic and feedback.
  5. Week 3 lesson 1: calculated percentages, concatenated labels and aliases.

Database development and evaluation

Build and test a six-table workshop system with controlled changes, atomic operations and requirement-linked recovery evidence.

What you’ll learn

  • Clean/import data with documented decisions and rollback.

  • Test, recover and evaluate against measurable requirements.

1. Keep the project inside its workshop budget

Develop the fictional workshop-booking system introduced earlier. Core scope: six tables, a DBMS or console interaction, reports, controlled booking/attendance, one member import and evidence of testing/recovery. A GUI is not required. Exclude login, payments, real personal records, multi-site deployment and a production retention system.

Week 4 supplies four explicit development lessons. Week 5 has four project workshops, weeks 6–9 two each, and week 10 four: sixteen project lessons already embedded in the outline. The other two lessons each week 6–9 remain explicit security teaching. No essential core work depends on extensive homework.

2. Investigate and design measurable requirements

IDRequired outcomeEvidence
R1Create six related tables and reconcile diagram/dictionary/schemaKeys/references/domain checks and actual six-table inspection
R2Provide required read-only reportsFour-table join, grouped count and calculated/concatenated output
R3Book known member/session once, without exceeding capacityNormal/last-place/full/duplicate/unknown/date tests; rejection unchanged
R4Record or update attendance only for booked pairJoint-key reference; 0/1 validation; unrecorded distinct from absence
R5Clean and import a synthetic member batch atomicallyMapping/normalisation log; invalid/duplicate batch leaves all rows unchanged
R6Demonstrate controlled schema/data changesCREATE/ALTER/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/cascade/DROP lab; safe transaction boundary
R7Demonstrate recovery and evaluate fitnessKnown-good copy, integrity/reference checks, content/report comparison, limitations

Turn each requirement in the table into a check you can observe. For example, a full session must reject another booking and leave the data unchanged. A statement such as “the system works” is too vague to check.

Use these scenario rules: each member/session pair can occur once; every retained Booking row counts towards capacity; a booking date must not be after its session date. The reference does not model cancellation history, waiting lists or clashes between session times.

Keep the diagram, 17-field dictionary and schema together. When you justify a schema change, update all three. Explain primary keys, composite keys and joint foreign-key references. Show which dependencies you remove through normalisation.

Also label where each rule is enforced. A direct SQL insert can bypass the application's cross-row capacity check. This prototype does not add database enforcement for every business rule. A clear account of that limit is part of an accurate design.

3. Make controlled changes and verify effects

-- Run only in a fresh disposable copy of the design database.
-- Predict each operation; this lab ends with ROLLBACK, preserving starting data/schema.
BEGIN;
CREATE TABLE ScratchNote (NoteID INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, NoteText TEXT NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO ScratchNote VALUES (1,'temporary lab');
ALTER TABLE Member ADD COLUMN Notes TEXT;
UPDATE Member SET Notes='reviewed synthetic record' WHERE MemberID='M03';
SELECT MemberID,Notes FROM Member ORDER BY MemberID;
DELETE FROM Booking WHERE MemberID='M01' AND SessionID='S01';
SELECT * FROM Attendance ORDER BY SessionID,MemberID;
DROP TABLE ScratchNote;
ROLLBACK;
-- Member has no Notes column again; original booking/attendance remain.

CREATE defines a table; ALTER TABLE changes supported schema features; INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE change rows; DROP removes a table. MODIFY is not a SQLite table-alteration command. SQLite supports a defined set of ALTER operations; more complex changes may need a careful table-rebuild procedure. Read current documentation rather than assuming another DBMS’s syntax.

The scoped DELETE uses both booking keys; its attendance is removed by the declared cascade. ROLLBACK restores this lab’s original rows/schema. Do not drop or reset the project database to “fix” a query. Real history deletion requires a separately agreed retention/authorisation policy.

4. Clean an import without inventing data

Inspect the raw synthetic CSV before importing it. It contains spaces around values, a lowercase ID and a blank name. Keep this raw file so you can explain every change.

  1. Agree the mapping: trim IDs, convert them to uppercase and require M followed by two digits.
  2. Trim names and require 1–60 characters. Reject duplicate IDs and IDs already in the database.
  3. Record each correction or rejection. Do not invent a missing name.
  4. Validate the whole batch, then insert it in one transaction using bound parameters.

The agreed import is atomic: either the whole batch succeeds or none of it remains. A malformed row rejects the batch. A later database failure rolls back earlier inserts. The corrected CSV contains three valid new records.

Here, normalising input means putting it into an agreed format. That does not establish accuracy or authenticity. You still need evidence about the source, age, relevance and unusual values.

5. Use transactions to protect a booking

Scope: implementation. ACID is required Year 12 knowledge. BEGIN, COMMIT and ROLLBACK illustrate an implementation in the chosen SQLite tool; they are not a separate additional prescribed keyword list. Teach tool behaviour before requiring it locally. Scope and source.

Treat “check for a place, then insert a booking” as one logical operation. If another writer can book between those steps, both requests might claim the final place. A transaction groups database work within a controlled boundary.

  • Atomicity: commit the whole logical change, or undo it.
  • Consistency: preserve the declared constraints and application rules.
  • Isolation: manage how transactions interact.
  • Durability: preserve committed changes under the configured storage guarantees. An in-memory demonstration cannot show survival after the process exits.

The example uses SQLite BEGIN IMMEDIATE to start a write transaction before counting bookings. Another writer cannot change the count between that check and insert. A busy or locking failure is still possible and needs a defined user response. The reference expects no active caller transaction and controls commit and rollback explicitly.

Do not assume one failed SQL statement undoes every earlier statement. Roll back the intended operation when it fails. Bound parameters keep data separate from SQL structure; they do not validate dates, capacity or permissions. The reference separately parses ISO calendar dates and checks the stored session date.

Python sqlite3 is a DB-API interface to SQLite. It is not an ODBC driver. ODBC is a separate standard, driver-based route from an application to a DBMS. Name the connection method your implementation actually uses.

Before you start: one SQL statement is one database command. A booking request can require several statements. Decide which statements belong to the same all-or-nothing operation before you write the error handling.

  1. Begin: open the transaction before reading a value that another writer could change.
  2. Check and change: count bookings, check the rules and carry out the linked inserts or updates inside that boundary.
  3. Commit on success: finalise the transaction only after every required step succeeds.
  4. Roll back on rejection or error: undo the operation's uncommitted changes. Do not continue to the success commit after an error.

Why begin before counting? Imagine one place remains. Without a protected check-and-insert sequence, requests A and B can both read “one place left” before either inserts. Both might then book it. In this SQLite reference, BEGIN IMMEDIATE obtains the write transaction first. Another writer cannot change the booking count between this check and insert. If the transaction cannot start because another writer is active, handle the busy result; do not use an old count as permission to insert.

For a two-step booking-and-attendance operation, a failed attendance statement does not by itself prove the earlier booking insert was undone. The application must roll back the intended operation. After rollback, compare the stored rows with the starting state. The code below is a transaction outline; the reference handles the checks and errors around it.

Read the reference functions before combining them. book() commits its own booking transaction; set_attendance() starts a separate transaction. Calling one after the other does not make both changes one atomic operation. A later attendance failure cannot roll back an already committed booking. To practice the combined operation, plan one shared transaction around both changes rather than nesting the existing functions, which expect no active caller transaction.

BEGIN IMMEDIATE;
-- Check known member/session, duplicate pair and current booking count.
-- If count < capacity, INSERT using parameters.
COMMIT;
-- On rejection/error, ROLLBACK the entire operation.

Visual walkthrough

A failed two-step change rolls back

In an illustrative operation, you try to book M03 into S02 and then record attendance. Both steps belong to one explicit transaction.

Pause and predict: Why must you inspect Booking after the failed attendance insert, rather than checking only the error message?

Show the explanation

The message shows that attendance failed. You still need evidence that the earlier booking insert was undone and unrelated rows stayed unchanged. That checks the transaction boundary.

Try a small change: Change the operation to a three-row import whose final insert fails. Explain which earlier inserts should remain after the agreed all-or-none rollback.

6. Test workflows, failures and reports

Start each test with a known dataset. This setup is a fixture. S01 has capacity 2 and already has two bookings, so a request for M03/S01 must be rejected without changing the database. S02 has capacity 3 and initially one booking, so M03/S02 can succeed once.

  1. Repeat M03/S02 and check that the duplicate is rejected.
  2. Try unknown IDs and late or invalid dates.
  3. Compare the full stored state before and after each rejection.
  4. Test attendance insertion and updates for a booked pair, invalid Boolean values and an unbooked pair.

For an import, try malformed IDs, IDs that become duplicates after normalising, and existing IDs. Trigger a later insert failure and check that earlier batch inserts are rolled back. After valid changes, predict and rerun the report rows and counts.

A passing test of one component does not show the whole user workflow. To check a requirement, follow the actual sequence the user needs and record its observed result.

7. Preserve a known-good version and prove recovery

Make a known-good copy before testing recovery. Keep the source/schema version and a test record with it. A backup is a recoverable copy; a restore test shows that you can use that copy again.

  1. Choose a suitable backup method. SQLite's backup API can copy a consistent state from an open database.
  2. Restore into a separate disposable destination so you preserve your current work.
  3. Reopen the restored database.
  4. Compare integrity checks, foreign-key checks, key counts, contents and required reports.
  5. Record the results and remaining limits.

Do not casually copy just one file from an active SQLite WAL database: required state may be in other files. Use an appropriate backup method or a controlled closed-database workflow.

The supplied demonstration copies into another in-memory connection and compares integrity, references and table contents. This checks copy behaviour. It does not demonstrate backup placement on disk, survival after exit or a saved-file restore. You need separate evidence for those claims.

10. Data quality: five factors in practice

Can you trust these values for this report? Use the dated source records to decide, then explain your choices. This is optional practice with explained answers.

Prepare a preliminary report on equipment owned by the fictional Harbour Learning Centre, using evidence available on 14 October 2026. Use one row per EquipmentID, quantities in individual items, non-negative whole-number quantities and explicit observation dates. This is an inventory report, not a supplier-stock list, price comparison or guarantee that equipment will be available for a future session.

All organisations, records, dates and verification notes in this exercise are fictional. Treat the source-card checks as supplied scenario facts, not real authentication evidence. The raw CSV is a manually compiled working copy and can contain copying errors even when its cited source is genuine. Blank means unknown, not zero. A’s reference counts are the best supplied inventory observations, but stock movements after 10 October are not documented.

Five questions to ask of data

FactorWhat to askEvidence to consider
AccuracyDo the values agree with the best available evidence?Compare with the source record; explain any mismatch.
CurrencyAre the observations recent enough for this purpose?Separate observation date from download date; consider changes since collection.
RelevanceDoes the data describe what this decision needs?Check population, location, time period, units and intended use.
AuthenticityIs the source or record what it claims to be?Check provenance through an established channel; a filename or plausible format is insufficient.
OutliersWhich unusual values need investigation in their context?Check units, source and circumstances; retain genuine extremes and flag unresolved ones.

Worked example: a valid-looking value can be wrong

R03 says there are 80 microphones. That is a valid non-negative integer, so it passes the format and range checks. But source A’s E03 record says 8. The copied value is inaccurate.

Use 8 in the report and record A:E03 as your evidence. Keep the original 80 in the raw data so someone can follow the correction. Label the observation 10 October, not the date you downloaded the file: that distinction matters for currency.

A’s verified origin supports authenticity, but does not prevent a copying mistake. Its count is relevant because it describes centre-owned equipment in individual items. Investigate an unusual value rather than deleting it automatically: the 240 chairs in R06 have supporting recount evidence.

1. Define fitness for purpose

What belongs in this inventory report? What remains uncertain even after cleaning?

Show explained answer

Use centre-owned stock, one row per EquipmentID, quantities in items and dated evidence. The cleaned example describes the supplied 10 October stocktake, not guaranteed stock on 14 or 20 October. Undocumented movements, condition and reservations remain uncertain. Data quality depends on this purpose.

2. Accuracy versus validation

Why is R03 inaccurate even though 80 is a non-negative integer? What evidence supports a correction?

Show explained answer

Format/domain validation can accept 80. The supplied A:E03 reference says 8 microphones, establishing a copying mismatch. Correct to 8 with a decision-log entry; do not claim integer validation proved factual accuracy.

3. Currency and dates

R04 was downloaded on 14 October 2026. Is its value of 6 tablets current? Which supplied observation should the report use?

Show explained answer

R04’s observation is from 1 November 2025; the recent download does not refresh it. A:E04 records 7 tablets on 10 October 2026. Use the newer observation with its actual date and source, preserving the old B record as history. Four-day-old evidence can still need a new stocktake for a time-critical decision.

4. Authenticity and provenance

Does the name Inventory_FINAL_verified.csv prove R09 and R12 are authentic? Name two checks you would request.

Show explained answer

No. Request the original record through an established centre channel and confirm who supplied it and how it was produced. Reconcile it with an approved stocktake or responsible custodian. A checksum is useful only against a trusted expected value and does not prove the inventory facts are true. Hold both rows while provenance and scope remain unresolved.

5. Relevance is a separate decision

Source C is recent and obtained through an established supplier channel. Why is R10 excluded? Could C be relevant for another task?

Show explained answer

R10 reports supplier warehouse stock, not equipment owned by the centre. Its provenance and age do not fix this scope mismatch. It could help investigate a purchasing decision, after checking product, unit, price and availability details for that new purpose.

6. Check units before comparing

R05 says 3 packs. Use A and D to express this quantity in the report’s unit. What would you do without D?

Show explained answer

A records three sealed packs and D confirms four matching kits per pack: 3 × 4 = 12 individual kits. Record both evidence references. Without a verified matching pack size, retain the raw unit and hold conversion pending clarification; do not assume one pack equals one item.

7. Missing and impossible values

What should happen to R07’s −2 webcams and R08’s blank quantity? Why is replacing both with zero wrong?

Show explained answer

Negative physical counts fail the specified domain; a blank is unknown. A:E07 supplies 12 webcams and A:E08 supplies 9 extension leads, so those corrections can be justified and logged. Zero would invent a fact. Without the references, hold the rows for clarification rather than guessing.

8. Handle a duplicate transparently

Should R02 and R11 both contribute to the projector count? Explain your decision and what you keep.

Show explained answer

No: this report requires one row per equipment ID, and the records duplicate the same observation and source. Use R02 once, suppress R11 in the report and keep both original rows plus the decision log. Do not apply a universal delete-duplicates rule to unrelated transaction data, where repeated events may be legitimate.

9. Investigate two possible outliers

Compare R06’s 240 chairs with R12’s 120 3D printers. What should be retained, and what needs investigation?

Show explained answer

Retain R06’s 240: A and the independent E recount support it, with a community-event explanation. Hold R12 because the source and context are unverified. Do not silently drop either row or change 120 to 12. Equipment categories have different typical quantities, so one numerical threshold across all categories would be misleading.

10. Apply all five factors

Complete a matrix with one piece of evidence, a conclusion or uncertainty, and a next action for each of the five factors.

Show explained answer

Example: accuracy—R03 differs from A:E03, correct 80 to 8; currency—B is an old observation, use A:E04 and disclose its date; relevance—C describes supplier stock, exclude from this inventory report; authenticity—U has unknown provenance, obtain an approved original; outliers—E confirms 240 chairs, retain with annotation while holding the unverified printer count. These judgements can overlap; they are not five independent pass/fail scores.

11. Build a defensible decision log

For every raw row, choose keep, correct/convert, supersede, hold, exclude or suppress duplicate. Which eight equipment IDs appear in the illustrative report?

Show explained answer

E01–E08 appear once each. Keep R01/R02; keep and annotate R06. Correct R03/R07, complete R08 from evidence, supersede R04 and convert R05. Hold R09/R12, exclude R10 for this purpose and suppress duplicate R11. The supplied decision-log CSV records references and reasons; the raw CSV remains unchanged.

12. Change the purpose

A coordinator wants to guarantee equipment availability for sessions on 20 October. Is the cleaned CSV enough? Apply all five factors to the new request.

Show explained answer

No. Seek a sufficiently recent stock/condition check (currency), reconcile actual usable counts (accuracy), collect session requirements and existing reservations (relevance), use approved records and verified custodians (authenticity), and investigate unusual changes or quantities (outliers). The current inventory observations do not establish future availability. Report the uncertainty rather than converting this worksheet’s illustrative data into an operational guarantee.

11. Verify a parameterised update at the interface

Use the example as a worked model, then fade the support: predict on paper, trace one execution together, change one requirement and test independently. What evidence shows that only the intended record changed?

import sqlite3
with sqlite3.connect(":memory:") as connection:
    connection.execute("PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON")
    connection.execute("CREATE TABLE Member (MemberID INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, Name TEXT NOT NULL)")
    connection.execute("INSERT INTO Member VALUES (?, ?)", (1, "O'Neil"))

12. Clean and manipulate a fictional event-log table

Clean for a stated purpose: summarise this fictional teaching service's events on 1 February 2027. S1 is a supplied trusted fixture export; U has unresolved provenance. EventID must be unique; UTC timestamps end in Z; approved hosts are LAB1–LAB3; durations are non-negative whole milliseconds. The supplied mapping permits ok → 200. Status 403/404/500 can be genuine evidence of denied access, missing resources or failures, not dirty data to erase.

Keep the raw 13 rows unchanged. First inspect them on paper. Normalise only documented equivalents (whitespace, host case and approved status aliases), validate formats/domains, distinguish exact duplicates from conflicting IDs, and hold unresolved rows. A missing duration is unknown, not zero. A very long duration may be genuine: retain and flag R08 for investigation. Do not make a security report look successful by deleting failed events.

StageStudent evidenceCheck
Inspect and predictRaw-row decision matrix with reasonsEvery raw row has a treatment
Clean without overwriting rawSeparate clean file plus decisionsConflicting L009 rows are both held
Manipulate for a reportFilter non-success events; group counts by host; total durationsDo not confuse row count, total and mean
Evaluate fitness for purposeReport retained/held counts and the long-duration flagState that excluded unresolved rows may change conclusions

Use the student log workbook, raw CSV and complete log lab. Teacher reference files and explanations are public learning resources. Source labels establish only this invented exercise's rules; they are not evidence about real school systems.

Pause and predict

Which of a missing duration, a genuine zero duration and a high duration should be treated as the same thing? Are matching IDs sufficient proof of duplicate events?

PYTHON 3 · WORKED EXAMPLE

Download clean_event_logs.py

"""Run beside event-logs-raw.csv in a disposable learning folder.
Fictional reference rules: EventID unique; trusted S1; UTC Z timestamps;
hosts LAB1..LAB3; approved 'ok' alias means 200; status 200/403/404/500;
duration is a non-negative integer; >1000 is reviewed, never auto-deleted.
Raw data is read only. Outputs go to separate worked-*.csv files.
"""
import csv
from datetime import datetime
from pathlib import Path

def normalise(row):
    if row["Source"] != "S1":
        raise ValueError("unverified source")
    event_id = row["EventID"].strip()
    if not event_id:
        raise ValueError("missing event ID")
    stamp = row["Timestamp"].strip()
    parsed = datetime.strptime(stamp, "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ")
    if parsed.strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ") != stamp:
        raise ValueError("timestamp must use the stated canonical format")
    stamp = parsed.strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ")
    host = row["Host"].strip().upper()
    if host not in {"LAB1", "LAB2", "LAB3"}:
        raise ValueError("unknown host")
    status_text = row["Status"].strip().lower()
    status = 200 if status_text == "ok" else int(status_text)
    if status not in {200, 403, 404, 500}:
        raise ValueError("unknown status")
    duration = int(row["DurationMS"].strip())
    if duration < 0:
        raise ValueError("negative duration")
    return (event_id, stamp, host, status, duration, "S1")

def clean(rows):
    candidates, decisions = [], {}
    for row in rows:
        try:
            record = normalise(row)
        except ValueError:
            decisions[row["RawRow"]] = ("hold", "verify source, format or domain against rules")
        else:
            candidates.append((row["RawRow"], record))
    versions = {}
    for raw_id, record in candidates:
        versions.setdefault(record[0], set()).add(record)
    kept, seen = [], set()
    for raw_id, record in candidates:
        if len(versions[record[0]]) > 1:
            decisions[raw_id] = ("hold", "conflicting records share an event ID")
        elif record in seen:
            decisions[raw_id] = ("suppress duplicate", "same normalised event already retained")
        else:
            kept.append(record)
            seen.add(record)
            note = "review unusually long duration; preserve original value" if record[4] > 1000 else "matches stated rules after documented normalisation"
            decisions[raw_id] = ("keep", note)
    return kept, [(row["RawRow"],) + decisions[row["RawRow"]] for row in rows]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    folder = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
    with (folder / "event-logs-raw.csv").open(newline="", encoding="utf-8") as source:
        rows = list(csv.DictReader(source))
    kept, decisions = clean(rows)
    for filename, header, records in [
        ("worked-clean.csv", ["EventID", "Timestamp", "Host", "Status", "DurationMS", "Source"], kept),
        ("worked-decisions.csv", ["RawRow", "Decision", "Reason"], decisions),
    ]:
        with (folder / filename).open("w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as output:
            writer = csv.writer(output)
            writer.writerow(header)
            writer.writerows(records)
    print("Retained", len(kept))
    print("Non-success", sum(record[3] != 200 for record in kept))
    print("Total duration", sum(record[4] for record in kept))
Show expected output after your prediction
Retained 6
Non-success 2
Total duration 10046

Build understanding in steps

  1. Guided completion: In pairs, annotate R01–R04 and agree normalised fields. Continue independently for the remaining rows, recording evidence and unresolved questions. Compare decisions before viewing the worked output.
  2. Independent transfer: Create a clean output and decision log, filter retained non-success events, then group retained events by host. Change one input to create an unknown host and rerun from the untouched raw copy. Explain how the report changes and what remains uncertain.
  3. Delayed retrieval: Using a fresh log with a different purpose, decide which cleaning rules still apply. Explain why a report of successful requests only cannot answer a question about all attempted access.
Show the explanation and checking guidance

The worked rules retain L001, L002, L003, L007, L010 and L011. R03 is an exact normalised duplicate. R05/R06/R07/R09 are held for missing/invalid/unverified data. R10 and R11 are both held because L009 conflicts. There are 6 retained rows, 2 non-success events and 2 retained events per host. Total duration is 10046 ms; the 9999 ms event strongly affects the total and must be reported, not guessed away.

13. DDL and DML: change the structure, change the records

DDL changes database structure: CREATE TABLE defines a table, ALTER TABLE changes supported parts of its structure, and DROP TABLE removes a table. DML changes stored records: INSERT adds rows, UPDATE changes matching rows and DELETE removes matching rows. SELECT retrieves data; some classifications call it DQL, while others include retrieval within DML. State the operation's effect rather than relying only on a label.

OperationExample purposeEvidence to inspect
CREATE / ALTERAdd the Item schema and an Active fieldColumn definitions, defaults and rejected invalid data
INSERTAdd two identified itemsKeys, row count and relationship validity
UPDATE ... WHEREChange the cable price onlyTarget record and unchanged camera record
DELETE ... WHERERemove the disposable cable fixtureIts absence and other records' survival
ROLLBACKUndo a trial price changePreviously committed value restored
DROP TABLERemove the Scratch structureTable no longer exists; unlike DELETE, it does not retain an empty table

Run the download only in a fresh disposable SQLite database. Predict the affected rows before modifying data and SELECT the target plus a non-target afterwards. A WHERE clause can still be wrong: its presence alone is not proof of correctness. SQLite uses ALTER TABLE for supported structural changes; do not paste another DBMS's MODIFY syntax without checking its documentation. Transactions manage a related change; authorisation, validation and constraints remain separate responsibilities.

Pause and predict

After the trial camera price update is rolled back, is its price 0 or 40? Does DELETE remove the Item table?

SQLITE · WORKED EXAMPLE

Download ddl_dml_lab.sql

-- Run on a fresh disposable SQLite database, not a school production database.
PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;
CREATE TABLE Supplier (
    SupplierID INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    SupplierName TEXT NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE Item (
    ItemID INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    ItemName TEXT NOT NULL,
    Cost REAL NOT NULL CHECK (Cost >= 0),
    SupplierID INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES Supplier(SupplierID)
);
ALTER TABLE Item ADD COLUMN Active INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1 CHECK (Active IN (0, 1));
INSERT INTO Supplier VALUES (1, 'North Supplies'), (2, 'West Supplies');
INSERT INTO Item (ItemID, ItemName, Cost, SupplierID)
VALUES (1, 'Camera', 40, 1), (2, 'Cable', 10, 1);
UPDATE Item SET Cost = 12 WHERE ItemID = 2;
DELETE FROM Item WHERE ItemID = 2 AND ItemName = 'Cable';
BEGIN TRANSACTION;
UPDATE Item SET Cost = 0 WHERE ItemID = 1;
ROLLBACK;
CREATE TABLE Scratch (Note TEXT);
DROP TABLE Scratch;
SELECT ItemID, ItemName, Cost, Active FROM Item ORDER BY ItemID;

Build understanding in steps

  1. Guided completion: Colour-code schema statements and record statements on paper. For each modification, identify target rows, expected state and one record/structure that should remain unchanged.
  2. Independent transfer: Use a fresh copy. Add an item, update only its cost, reject a negative cost using the constraint, and delete the disposable item. Inspect state after each operation. Compare DELETE FROM Scratch with DROP TABLE Scratch in separate fresh trials.
  3. Delayed retrieval: Without looking at the labels, explain what each SQL statement changes and design an unaffected-row test that would expose a missing or incorrect WHERE.
Show the explanation and checking guidance

The final Item row is (1, Camera, 40, 1). The cable row was removed; rollback restores the camera price. Supplier still contains two rows. Scratch has been dropped. A negative cost is rejected by CHECK and must not alter the previously stored valid row. DELETE changes rows; DROP removes the structure.
